case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the U.S. Air Force’s submission of a hazardous-waste permit renewal application (and related waste-disposal planning) is “final agency action” reviewable under the APA and, if so, whether NEPA requires environmental review notwithstanding the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) permitting scheme administered by Guam EPA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) final-agency-action requirement (5 U.S.C. § 704) as applied to NEPA compliance claims; National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) procedural requirements (42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C)); Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) hazardous-waste permitting framework (42 U.S.C. § 6901 et seq.) and related “displacement”/“functional equivalent” doctrines.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Air Force et al.) argue that the Ninth Circuit wrongly treated a permit-renewal application submitted to Guam EPA as reviewable “final agency action” because it imposes no direct legal consequences until Guam EPA acts, making it analogous to nonfinal submissions in Franklin v. Massachusetts and Dalton v. Specter. They further contend NEPA should not apply (or is effectively displaced) in this context because the RCRA permitting process supplies the relevant procedural safeguards and Congress did not intend duplicative NEPA review layered on top of specialized hazardous-waste permitting administered by a separate permitting authority.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Prutehi Guahan) argues the Ninth Circuit correctly found final agency action because the Air Force reached a consummated decision on a specific course of conduct for handling hazardous waste and committed itself to a plan that has practical and legal consequences, making the controversy ripe for review under Bennett v. Spear’s finality framework. Respondent also argues NEPA applies and is not displaced by RCRA here: RCRA’s permitting procedures (especially as implemented by Guam EPA) are not a categorical substitute for NEPA’s environmental review obligations, and nothing in RCRA shows congressional intent to make NEPA compliance superfluous for federal agencies undertaking actions with significant environmental effects.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress the serious real-world consequences of allowing OB/OD to continue during the permitting process, but under Bennett v. Spear those practical effects do not substitute for the required legal consequences flowing from the challenged agency action itself. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, whatever legal authorization to continue operations (or any binding constraints) exists turns on Guam EPA’s permitting decision, so the Air Force’s submission is best understood as a nonfinal step akin to the submissions/recommendations in Franklin and Dalton. Treating an application as “final agency action” would collapse § 704’s finality line and invite premature NEPA litigation over intermediate paperwork, contrary to Lujan’s insistence on discrete, legally operative agency action. A narrow holding on finality preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves open NEPA review when a concrete, legally binding permit decision or federal approval actually fixes rights and obligations.

Spear’s second prong asks whether the challenged federal act itself determines rights or obligations or produces legal consequences—not whether it predictably perpetuates a harmful status quo. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, any binding authorization to continue (or constraints on) OB/OD activity flows from Guam EPA’s discretionary permit decision, making the Air Force’s filing analogous to the nonfinal submissions in Franklin v. Massachusetts and Dalton v. Specter. Under a textualist reading of APA § 704, treating an application to another sovereign as “final agency action” would collapse the statute’s finality limit and invite premature NEPA suits over intermediate paperwork. NEPA review, if available, should await a discrete federal action with independent legal effect (or a final permitting decision that actually fixes legal consequences).

Justice Kagan’s reliance on Lujan’s “discrete agency action” requirement does not defeat review in my view because the application is itself discrete and consummated; categorically labeling it nonfinal would let federal actors evade NEPA by routing major federal action through territorial permitting while continuing harmful operations. Absent a clear statement that RCRA displaces NEPA here, I would not read § 704 finality to insulate this kind of ongoing, federally driven environmental impact from judicial scrutiny.

NEPA’s real-world focus does not let us rewrite the APA’s finality boundary, and any NEPA challenge can be brought when there is a final permitting action or other federal act with independent legal effect.

Sotomayor’s contention that continued operation pending renewal is a “consequence” of the federal filing still traces legally to Guam’s regulatory regime, not a definitive federal determination, and accepting her baseline-setting theory would drift toward the kind of non-discrete, intermediary planning challenge we cautioned against in Lujan. A narrow holding on nonfinality preserves later NEPA challenges to any truly operative federal action while avoiding premature judicial intrusion into an ongoing permitting process.

Spear, which asks whether the challenged federal act itself carries legal consequences, not whether it predictably influences later choices. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, any operative authority to continue operating and any change in legal rights or obligations flows from Guam EPA’s regulatory scheme and its intervening discretionary permit decision, paralleling Franklin and Dalton’s break-in-finality logic. Treating an application as final agency action would untether finality from text and convert § 704 into a broad practical-effects test—an approach inconsistent with Lujan’s rejection of judicial review over intermediary steps lacking discrete legal effect. As the Chief Justice notes (and Justice Kagan reinforces), this filing is an initiating submission to a separate permitting sovereign whose intervening discretionary decision breaks finality under the logic of Franklin and Dalton; whatever on-the-ground continuation occurs stems from Guam’s regulatory regime, not a definitive federal determination fixing rights or obligations. Sotomayor’s “baseline-setting/status quo” theory is too close to the programmatic-planning concerns Lujan warned against, and accepting it would invite premature NEPA litigation over routine paperwork filings and disrupt permitting processes without any operative federal action to review. NEPA timing concerns cannot justify relaxing § 704’s jurisdictional boundary; review must wait for a discrete federal action with concrete legal effect (if one exists).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Franklin/Dalton analogy is the strongest point for Petitioner, but those cases involved recommendations to a separate federal decisionmaker whose discretion severed legal effect; here the Air Force’s renewal submission predictably triggers continued authorization to operate under the existing regime and concretely shapes the permitting baseline in a way that carries practical—and in context, regulatory—consequences on the ground. Section 704 finality should not be read to make NEPA review impossible until after an agency is practically locked in, particularly where the affected community bears the environmental and health risks during the extended operating period.
